label: Chapter 1
name: An Overview of Supply Chain and Logistics Management

questions.q: In the Li & Fung jacket example, which pairing of country and contribution is correct?
questions.d: Li & Fung sourced one jacket from five countries and had it stitched in Thailand. China made the liner (cotton), Thailand ringed the hood with imitation fur, Japan put the teeth in the zipper (stainless steel), Germany sent the snaps, and Taiwan produced the shell and fleece.

questions.q: According to the slides' definition, supply chain management works to control, manage and improve the flow of:
o: Material and information, from the suppliers to the end users
Cash only, from customers back to suppliers
Finished goods only, from factories to retailers
People and equipment between a company's departments
questions.d: SCM unifies a network of connected but interdependent organisations, working together to control, manage and improve the flow of material and information from the suppliers to the end users, while increasing value to the end users at less cost as a whole.

questions.q: Purchasing, production, inventory, transportation and sales are best described as:
o: Activities that have to be managed across the supply chain, not the supply chain itself
Activities each department should manage separately
Activities that matter to logistics but not to SCM
questions.d: SCM coordinates the many activities involved in creating and delivering a product. These activities are not themselves 'the supply chain'; they are activities that have to be managed across the supply chain.

questions.q: Which period do the slides link to the development of MRP and MRPII?
questions.d: 1960s–1970s: new computer technologies led to Materials Requirements Planning (MRP) and Manufacturing Resource Planning (MRPII), used to coordinate inventory management and improve internal communications.

questions.q: In the 1950s–1960s, U.S. manufacturers' main strategy for cutting costs and improving productivity was:
questions.d: 1950s–1960s: U.S. manufacturers focused on mass production techniques as their principal cost reduction and productivity improvement strategies.

questions.q: Which approach aligns raw-material orders from suppliers directly with production schedules?
questions.d: JIT is an inventory management strategy that aligns raw-material orders from suppliers directly with production schedules. It is one of the 1980s–1990s developments, along with TQM, BPR and CRM.

questions.q: Business process reengineering (BPR) aimed to help organisations:
o: Fundamentally rethink how they do their work to improve service, cut costs and become world-class competitors
Continually detect and reduce errors in manufacturing
Manage and analyse interactions with past, current and potential customers
Match raw-material orders to production schedules
questions.d: BPR aimed to help organisations fundamentally rethink how they do their work to improve customer service, cut operational costs and become world-class competitors. Continual error reduction is TQM, and managing customer interactions is CRM.

questions.q: Which group of initiatives do the slides place in '2000s and beyond'?
o: Third-party service providers (3PLs), integrating logistics, and client/server ERP software
questions.d: 2000s and beyond focused on improving supply chain capabilities through third-party service providers (3PLs), integrating logistics, and client/server SCM software such as Enterprise Resource Planning.

questions.q: The 'triple bottom line' means taking care of:
questions.d: Today the emphasis is on the environmental and social impacts of supply chains. The triple bottom line means taking care of people, planet and profits.

questions.q: According to the CLM definition, logistics management plans, implements and controls:
o: The efficient, effective forward and reverse flow and storage of goods, services and related information between origin and consumption
Only the forward flow of finished goods to customers
The financial flows between supply chain partners
The design of new products together with suppliers
questions.d: Logistics management is the part of SCM that plans, implements and controls the efficient, effective forward and reverse flow and storage of goods, services and related information between the point of origin and the point of consumption to meet customers' requirements.

questions.q: What is the goal of logistics according to the slides?
o: A target level of customer service at the lowest possible cost
The highest possible service level, whatever the cost
Holding as much inventory as possible to avoid stockouts
Using as few suppliers as possible
questions.d: The goal of logistics is to achieve a target level of customer service at the lowest possible cost.

questions.q: Which definition of logistics is credited to Donald Waters (Global Logistics, 2010)?
o: The function responsible for moving materials through their supply chain
Managing the flow of items, information, cash and ideas by adding place, period and pattern values
The part of SCM that controls forward and reverse flows between origin and consumption
A network of organisations working together to improve material and information flows
questions.d: Donald Waters: logistics is the function responsible for moving materials through their supply chain. The 'place, period and pattern values' definition is from MIT's Center for Transportation & Logistics, and the forward/reverse flow definition is from CLM.

questions.q: According to the slides, which firms gain the most from successful SCM?
o: Firms that rely on a single supplier
Small firms that hold no inventory
Firms that manage each function separately
questions.d: Firms with large system inventories gain the most from successful SCM. SCM reduces safety stocks and costs through coordinated planning and better information sharing, leading to lower purchasing and carrying costs, better quality, higher service levels, and higher sales and profits.

questions.q: A bakery turns flour, sugar and eggs into cakes its customers can eat. Which economic utility does this create?
questions.d: Form utility: a product is in a form that can be used by the customer and is of value to them. The four types of economic utility are possession, form, time and place.

questions.q: Moving products from points of lesser value to points of greater value creates:
questions.d: Place utility means having products available where customers need them; products are moved from points of lesser value to points of greater value.

questions.q: A retailer makes sure school uniforms arrive in the weeks just before the school year starts, when parents need them. This mainly creates:
questions.d: Time utility means having products available when customers need them. Place utility is about where they are available.

questions.q: The four types of economic utility are possession, form, time and price.
questions.d: The four types are possession, form, time and place. Price is not one of them.

questions.q: Logistics and SCM can be managed as isolated functions because they rarely cross borders.
questions.d: Logistics and SCM span across the globe and cannot be managed as an isolated function. They connect functions, divisions and business units within and across firms.

questions.q: Historically, purchasing, production, inventory, transportation and sales were often managed separately.
questions.d: Companies did not always manage these activities in an integrated way. Historically they were often managed separately, which led to the integrated concept now called SCM.

questions.q: Sustainability means meeting the needs of current supply chain members without hindering the ability to meet the needs of future generations.
questions.d: That is the slides' definition of sustainability, part of today's emphasis on the environmental and social impacts of supply chains.
